old: The jump from tier 3 to tier 4 is where most teams stall, and it's the one that actually matters most for non-determinism specifically. If your system has genuine run-to-run variance, evaluating each golden-set item once and reporting '87% pass rate' hides whether that 87% is stable or whether a single re-run would show 79%. Sampling k responses per test case (say k=5) and reporting pass@k or a mean with a confidence interval turns 'did we regress' from a guess into a testable statistical claim, and lets you set CI gates like 'fail the build only if the lower bound of the 95% CI drops below the previous release's lower bound' instead of an arbitrary single-number threshold that trips on noise every other week.
new: Repeated trials are useful only if the metric matches the deployment policy. Report per-attempt success separately from pass@k (at least one success in k attempts), along with latency, cost and how an answer is selected. With independent 50%-successful attempts, pass@5 is 96.875% while per-attempt reliability is still 50%; real attempts may be correlated. Compare baseline and candidate on the same representative cases. Define a tolerated degradation or meaningful improvement in advance, then use a paired comparison and an uncertainty estimate appropriate to repeated measurements. Comparing two lower confidence bounds alone is not a sound regression test.

old: A golden dataset isn't a handful of examples you wrote in an afternoon — it's a living, stratified sample that should track your actual failure taxonomy. Start by mining real production traffic (with appropriate privacy handling): the queries users actually send are a very different distribution from what a PM imagines during a demo. Bucket examples by failure category you care about — hallucination under sparse retrieval, refusal on borderline-but-legitimate requests, formatting breakage, multi-turn context loss, adversarial jailbreak attempts — and make sure each bucket has enough examples that a regression in that specific failure mode is statistically visible, not just a couple of anecdotal misses. A 20-example golden set can't reliably detect a change from a 5% to an 8% failure rate on some subcategory; the confidence interval on a proportion from n=20 is enormous. You typically need low hundreds of examples per category you're tracking before a CI gate on that category means anything.
new: A golden dataset should reflect actual tasks and consequential failure categories, with privacy-safe examples and labels. Keep development examples separate from held-out evaluation cases. Choose sample sizes based on the baseline error rate, effect size, uncertainty and decision stakes: there is no universal ‘low hundreds per category’ rule. A 20-example sample cannot reliably distinguish a 5% from an 8% error rate; detecting a small change may require far more data than a few hundred cases. For small datasets, report exact error counts and the uncertainty rather than claiming a stable percentage. Refresh the set as real failures and user tasks change.

old: The tradeoff most practitioners miss is symmetric vs. asymmetric search. Many embedding models are trained for symmetric similarity (sentence A vs. sentence B, same length and style), but RAG is fundamentally asymmetric: a short, terse query ("retry count for payment webhook") is being matched against long, discursive documentation. If your embedding model wasn't trained for this asymmetry, the query vector and the correct document vector can end up further apart than the query and a completely wrong but similarly-phrased document. This is why production-grade embedding models (e.g., the E5, BGE, or OpenAI's text-embedding-3 families) are explicitly trained with query/passage pairs and often require prefixing input with 'query: ' or 'passage: ' at inference time — omitting that prefix, which is an easy integration mistake, measurably degrades retrieval quality and shows no error anywhere in your stack.
new: Query-to-passage retrieval is often asymmetric: a short question must match a longer explanatory document. Evaluate embedding models on that task, not just paraphrase similarity. Input conventions are model-specific. E5 models commonly document query: and passage: prefixes; BGE variants may use their own query instructions; other services do not require either convention. Follow the exact model/version documentation rather than applying one family's prefix rule to E5, BGE and OpenAI embeddings interchangeably. Compare against a keyword baseline and measure retrieval on labeled queries before changing the model.

old: **Native function/tool calling** is a different, complementary mechanism. You don't just hand the model a schema for its final answer — you register one or more named tools (each with a JSON Schema for its arguments) as part of the API call. The model is trained to recognize when the user's request warrants invoking one of these, and instead of writing prose it emits a distinct structured content block (Anthropic calls it a `tool_use` block) containing the tool name and schema-conformant arguments, along with a stop reason indicating it's pausing for you to act. Critically: **the model never executes anything.** Your application code reads the tool_use block, runs the real function against your real systems, and sends the result back as a new message. The model only ever produces the *intent* to call a function with certain arguments — execution, authorization, and side effects are entirely your application's responsibility.
new: **Native function/tool calling** registers named tools and argument schemas so a model can propose a call, for example as a tool_use block. Ordinary tool calling does not universally guarantee schema-conformant arguments; strict modes and supported schema features depend on the provider and model. Validate arguments and handle refusals, incomplete output and unknown tools. The model proposes intent; application code enforces authorization, checks authoritative state, executes permitted actions and returns results. Execution and side effects remain the application's responsibility.

old: **Native function/tool calling** — the model chooses whether to act at all, and which of possibly several tools to invoke, then produces schema-conformant arguments for that specific tool. This is the only mechanism that models "the model can decide not to call anything" and "the model can pick between N different actions" cleanly — which is exactly the shape of most agentic and assistant-style features. It costs you the orchestration complexity of the loop above: matching tool_use ids to results, handling the case where the model requests several tools in parallel, and deciding a `tool_choice` policy.
new: **Native function/tool calling** lets the model propose which tool to use, subject to the endpoint's tool-choice settings. An application can also route actions deterministically; tool calling is not the only possible control mechanism. Check the provider's actual guarantees for strict argument schemas. The application must manage tool IDs and results, parallel calls, validation errors, budgets and stop conditions independently of the model's proposal.

old: **Constrained decoding** (what powers "JSON mode" and schema-locked structured output) changes this at the sampling step itself. The provider compiles your JSON Schema into a grammar — conceptually a state machine describing every valid next token at every position in a well-formed instance of that schema. At each decoding step, the sampler masks out (sets to zero probability) every token that would violate the grammar, then samples only from what remains. This is why it can *guarantee* syntactic validity and, for the fields the grammar tracks, structural validity too — required keys will be present, enums will be members of the allowed set, types will match. It cannot guarantee the *values* are correct, because the grammar constrains form, not content.
new: **Constrained decoding** restricts allowed next tokens according to a grammar or supported schema. Distinguish basic JSON mode, which targets JSON syntax, from strict schema-constrained output. A provider's supported strict mode can enforce supported structural constraints, but it does not establish factual or business-rule correctness. Handle refusals and truncated responses separately, and validate against the exact supported schema rather than assuming full JSON Schema support.

old: **Schema-constrained decoding / JSON mode with a schema** — you pass a JSON Schema and the provider guarantees the output is valid JSON conforming to it via grammar-masked sampling. Great when you always want exactly one shaped object back and there's no decision about *whether* to act — pure extraction, classification, summarization into fields. Not all schema features are supported identically across providers (recursive schemas, certain `anyOf`/`oneOf` combinations, `pattern` regex, and deep nesting are common gaps), and constraining every token adds measurable latency versus free generation, so it's worth checking your provider's actual schema-feature support against what you're asking for rather than assuming full JSON Schema coverage.
new: **Strict schema-constrained output** is useful when the task always returns one shaped object. Check which schema features the provider supports and handle refusal, truncation and validation failures explicitly. Basic JSON mode is not the same guarantee: valid JSON can still omit required business fields or contain the wrong values. Benchmark latency for the selected model and schema instead of assuming a universal overhead.
